newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Britain faces showdown on EU working week battle.
newsitem.headline: Britain faces showdown on EU working week battle.

text.p: The European Union's top court is set to rule on Tuesday on a maximum working week that could further strain Britain's relationship with its EU partners.
The European Court of Justice will give its verdict on whether an EU law on working hours and rest periods should stand -- an issue that Prime Minister John Major has given high political priority.
Britain argues that a 1993 directive limiting the average work week to 48 hours in most sectors was adopted illegally and represents gross interference from Brussels.
"I don't think this is the sort of legislation that ought to emanate prescriptively from Europe," Major told BBC Radio last week.
If Britain loses in the Luxembourg-based court, he said, London will take its case to the inter-governmental conference (IGC) that is considering ways to amend the EU treaty.
Britain is already isolated on many issues under discussion in the IGC and another big fight could threaten to derail the negotiations beyond their planned end next June.
Major, however, won surprise support for his position on Friday, when French President Jacques Chirac said after a Franco-British summit that he was "very close to John Major in this matter".

Britain, still at odds with the EU over a ban on British beef imposed because of fears of mad cow disease, is pessimistic about its chances on Tuesday because an advocate-general of EU court -- a top legal adviser -- rejected its arguments in March.
However, while the court generally follows the opinions of its advocates-general, it is under no obligation to do so and could offer up a surprise.

In addition to setting the maximum work week, the EU directive limits night shifts to an average of eight hours and says everyone should have four weeks paid leave a year and at least one day off a week.
London challenged it on the grounds that it was adopted by EU ministers as a health and safety measure requiring only a majority vote, bypassing British attempts to block it.
It cited an EU treaty article requiring legislation affecting the "rights and interests of employed persons" to be adopted unanimously. This would have allowed London to block it.

Major told BBC Television last week that the law should not be imposed on Britain because the Social Protocol of the Maastricht Treaty, which took effect in 1993, gives it the right to opt out of EU workplace regulations.
But the court's advocate general said the EU law was indeed a health and safety measure, citing a treaty provision on that subject calling for improvements in the "working environment".

Referring to rest periods and a maximum work week, he said: "Without such guarantees, workers were exposed to the risk of frequently being required to work excessively long hours beyond their physical or psychological capabilities, thereby jeopardising their health and safety."

The European Commission vigorously defends the directive and wants to extend it to sectors that are now excluded -- in the road, rail, inland waterways and air transport sectors, workers at sea and doctors in training.
It plans to issue a policy paper on that question once it analyses the Court of Justice ruling.
